did_you_know.text: Did you know? The word "nehashim" (serpents/omens) in this verse refers to ancient practices of divination and sorcery, in which Balaam was an expert.

Did you know? The phrase "shtum ha'ayin" (sealed/opened/perfected eye) is enigmatic and translated differently, such as "closed eye," "open eye," or "perfect eye," highlighting Balaam's mysterious nature.
Did you know? The verse "Mah Tovu Ohalecha Yaakov" (How goodly are your tents, O Jacob) is a famous prayer recited when entering a synagogue, highlighting the beauty of order and community.
Did you know? "Agag" mentioned in this verse refers to future kings of Amalek, such as the one King Saul killed in the Book of Samuel, making Balaam's prophecy long-term.
Did you know? The "Re'em" mentioned in this verse was a strong and powerful animal in the ancient world, symbolizing might and ferocity, sometimes translated as "wild ox" or "unicorn."
Did you know? "A star from Jacob" is one of the most famous messianic prophecies in the Bible, interpreted throughout generations as referring to an important leader or the coming Messiah.

Did you know? The epithet "first of the nations" for Amalek in this verse likely refers to them being the first to attack the Israelites after their exodus from Egypt, rather than their chronological antiquity.
Did you know? The Kenites were a nomadic tribe, likely metalworkers (their name "Kain" is related to "smith"), and often allied with Israel, like Jethro, Moses' father-in-law.
